question: What changes when a familiar melodic contour returns in a different orchestral setting?
intro: A flute traces a line before the orchestra supplies its surroundings. Debussy’s response to Mallarmé’s poem grows through repeated contours, changing accompaniments and one broad central expansion, then returns to a quieter scale. Paul Paray conducts the Detroit Symphony Orchestra in Mercury’s historical mono recording.

sections.label: A · The flute’s changing surroundings
sections.mNote: Opening material expands through new accompaniments and wind exchanges.

sections.label: B · A sustained middle span
sections.mNote: Approximate approach to the score’s D♭-major middle, bars 55–78.

sections.label: A′ · Opening tempo recovered
sections.mNote: Flute and harp recover the opening manner; earlier wind ideas follow.

sections.label: Coda · The line remembered
sections.mNote: The opening contour returns, coloured by antique cymbals, before E-major repose.

cues.title: A flute before a harmony
cues.text: The opening flute line curls down and back up before the orchestra answers. Its first descent spans a tritone, an interval that does not settle comfortably into a major or minor chord. Follow the contour before trying to name a key.
cues.evidence: Fromont full score p.1, opening three unaccompanied bars: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/40/IMSLP14736-Debussy_-_Pr%C3%A9lude_%C3%A0_l%27apr%C3%A8s-midi_d%27un_faune_%28orch._score%29.pdf. The report places the quiet flute opening before the rise around 0:20; no exact note-to-second alignment is claimed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The same line, another setting
cues.text: Across the opening, listen for the flute’s contour against successive changes of accompaniment. A melody can remain recognisable while the harmony underneath changes its direction. The interest lies as much in the answer as in the opening call.
cues.evidence: The changing settings of the opening theme are described in the Pearson analysis, pp.2–5: https://qualifications.pearson.com/content/dam/pdf/A%20Level/Music/2013/Teaching%20and%20learning%20materials/Unit-3-5-Debussy.pdf. The 0:44 novelty peak is an approximate listening landmark, not a specified flute entrance.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A poem, not a plot
cues.text: Mallarmé’s poem appeared in 1876. Debussy does not turn it into a sequence of narrated incidents: the music offers a response to its atmosphere and images. The solo flute’s winding line remains a useful thread through that freely unfolding response.
cues.evidence: Kathy Henkel, LA Phil programme note, on Mallarmé’s 1876 poem and Debussy’s description of his musical illustration: https://www.laphil.com/works/prelude-to-the-afternoon-of-a-faun-l-86. This context concerns the work, not an event at this timestamp.

cues.title: Pressure released
cues.text: After an early swell, the sound drops away and leaves room around the line again. Compare the weight of the orchestral response with the much lighter space that follows it; the piece repeatedly grows without staying at its new level.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/debussy-faune.txt: relative level rises to −6.5 dB around 1:25, then falls to −27.2 dB around 1:35 and stays comparatively low through 1:50. The cue follows that broad withdrawal.

cues.title: Listen below the tune
cues.text: Debussy often divides the strings rather than asking each section to move as one block. Listen for a sustained background and small inner movements beneath a wind phrase: an orchestral colour can contain several separate lines.
cues.evidence: Pearson analysis p.2 and the Fromont score document divided and muted strings: https://qualifications.pearson.com/content/dam/pdf/A%20Level/Music/2013/Teaching%20and%20learning%20materials/Unit-3-5-Debussy.pdf. This is a movement-wide listening invitation, not an isolated instrumental entrance at 2:30.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The first performance
cues.text: Gustave Doret conducted the première in Paris on 22 December 1894. Debussy’s score asks for a modest brass presence—four horns, but no trumpets or trombones—within an orchestra whose winds and harps carry much of the changing colour.
cues.evidence: Première and scoring: IMSLP work catalogue https://imslp.org/wiki/Prelude_a_l%27apres-midi_d%27un_faune_(Debussy,_Claude); instrumentation also visible in the Fromont score.

cues.title: The central phrase approaches
cues.text: The middle of the piece offers a more sustained melodic span. Keep the opening’s short, winding gesture in memory and compare it with a line that seems to draw a longer breath. This is an expansion, not a march into a new tempo.
cues.evidence: Pearson analysis identifies bars 55–78 as the contrasting middle and a preceding four-bar dominant preparation. Report: the 3:30–3:35 swell retreats through 3:45–4:00, before the middle expansion. The boundary is approximate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A fuller stretch of sound
cues.text: The central span gathers more weight and sustains it across several phrases. Listen through the crest rather than treating each loud point as an arrival: the broad line carries on beyond the first increase in intensity.
cues.evidence: Report: the loudest five-second windows include 4:25 and 4:50; relative level remains comparatively high between 4:20 and 4:55. No instrument or chord is identified from loudness alone.

cues.title: A middle that can withdraw
cues.text: The central expansion does not end with a triumphant stop. Its energy subsides, preparing the return of the opening manner. The approaching change matters because Debussy can recover an earlier sound without repeating the whole opening literally.
cues.evidence: Pearson analysis, bars 55–78 and return at 79; Fromont score pp.20–21. The report falls after the 4:50 crest and marks a strong change at 5:24. Timing estimates the return rather than fixing a bar.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Flute and harp, remembered
cues.text: In the return, the flute again carries a gently curved line while the harp supplies flowing motion beneath it. Compare this supported recollection with the solitary flute at the start: recognition comes with a different background.
cues.evidence: Fromont score p.21, rehearsal 8, Mouvement du Début: flute, harp and divided strings. Report: novelty peak 5:24 and a quieter E-centred region at 5:25–5:40 support the broad placement, not an exact entrance.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: One LP, several sea pieces
cues.text: This transfer comes from Mercury MG 50101, a mono LP coupling the Faune with La Mer and Ibéria. The archive dates that issue to 1956. Its digital upload and its much earlier orchestral session are separate events in the recording’s history.
cues.evidence: Internet Archive item metadata and scanned label: https://archive.org/details/lp_ibria-la-mer-prelude-to-the-afternoon-of_paul-paray-claude-debussy-detroit-symphony. Eloquence session documentation identifies the Detroit sessions of December 1955: https://www.eloquenceclassics.com/releases-archive/paul-paray-the-mercury-masters-vol-2-1958-1962/

cues.title: A small metallic colour
cues.text: In the closing pages, antique cymbals add a light, pitched resonance rather than a large orchestral crash. Listen for the contrast between sustained wind tone and a struck sound that begins to decay as soon as it is made.
cues.evidence: Fromont score p.27, rehearsal 10, introduces cymbales antiques; the closing pages show their E and B pitches. The 6:30 novelty peak is used as a broad coda landmark; no isolated cymbal strike is timed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A clearer destination
cues.text: The score eventually settles into E major, but the opening has made that destination anything but obvious. Listen for the difference between recognising a familiar melodic shape and finally hearing the harmony come to rest.
cues.evidence: Pearson analysis p.4 identifies the E-major close and cadence in bars 105–106: https://qualifications.pearson.com/content/dam/pdf/A%20Level/Music/2013/Teaching%20and%20learning%20materials/Unit-3-5-Debussy.pdf. The cue anticipates the closing passage; it does not place that cadence at 7:25.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A quiet final resonance
cues.text: The closing passage stays quiet. Let the remaining resonance run its course rather than expecting one last orchestral surge: Debussy ends by reducing the pressure that the central span had accumulated.
cues.evidence: Report: 7:55–8:25 remains approximately −25 to −31 dB relative to the loudest frame. The Fromont score’s final page marks the close very slow and restrained. The cue concerns the whole withdrawal.

transitions.title: A longer breath replaces the winding gesture
transitions.how: The opening material has already changed its surroundings several times. The contrasting middle makes a more sustained melody prominent and establishes the D♭-major region after dominant preparation. Winds combine over a gently articulated string background. The join enlarges phrase and texture without a hard break; the new key matters because it gives the extended line a temporary place to settle.
transitions.evidence: Pearson analysis: bars 51–54 prepare D♭, bars 55–78 form the middle; Fromont score p.15. Report: retreat at 3:45–4:00 followed by the broader 4:20–4:55 crest; 4:02 is an approximate sectional boundary.

transitions.title: The flute recovers its earlier pace
transitions.how: The sustained middle phrase loses weight rather than being cut off. Debussy restores the opening tempo and brings flute, harp and held string harmony into focus. The flute’s recollection is now supported by a flowing accompaniment: a change of setting makes familiar material feel newly placed.
transitions.evidence: Fromont score p.21, rehearsal 8, Mouvement du Début; Pearson bars 79 onward. Report: strong novelty at 5:24, reduced level and changed pitch distribution at 5:25–5:40. This is a passage estimate.

transitions.title: The first contour becomes a quiet farewell
transitions.how: The later wind exchanges lead back to the opening flute contour with the instruction to play in the first tempo, but with more languor. Antique cymbals colour the recollection, and the strings continue softly below it. The familiar gesture now belongs to a closing process that will settle into E major, not to another full cycle of expansion.
transitions.evidence: Fromont score p.27, rehearsal 10, and final pages; Pearson bars 94–110. Report: novelty at 6:30 followed by a new pitch distribution; the coda marker is not bar-aligned.

source.title: Debussy, Prélude à l’après-midi d’un faune · Fromont full score, plate E. 1091 F.
source.locator: pp.1,15,21–23,27,31. Selected passage snapshots; except the opening, their placement is estimated from the report’s large-scale changes, not individual entrances.

timeline.note: A solitary first flute presents the opening contour.
The first orchestral answers introduce horns and harp around the flute line.
The middle melody is shared by high winds over a sustained string background.
At the recovery of the opening tempo, flute and flowing harp stand above held divided strings.
The later return includes an oboe phrase and softly moving horn accompaniment.
The opening flute contour is recalled with antique cymbals and quiet strings.
The final page combines soft winds, harp resonance, antique cymbals and a plucked low-string close.

composer.epithet: He made a chord’s spacing, a scale’s missing notes and an instrument’s register determine the course of a piece.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1872; piano with Antoine Marmontel, composition with Ernest Guiraud
Prix de Rome 1884 · Paris Exposition 1889 · Pelléas et Mélisande 1902
One completed opera, orchestral triptychs, piano collections, songs, a quartet and three late sonatas
French Symbolist poetry · Russian music · Javanese gamelan · eighteenth-century French keyboard music
composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, outside Paris. Neither parent was a professional musician. His father’s involvement in the Paris Commune brought imprisonment in 1871; through a connection made during that imprisonment, the boy came to the piano teacher Antoinette Mauté, Verlaine’s mother-in-law. He entered the Paris Conservatoire in 1872, aged ten. Antoine Marmontel trained him as a pianist; Ernest Guiraud later taught him composition. His resistance to harmonic rules developed inside this education: he could play, analyse and compete successfully in the system he came to distrust.

From 1880 he spent summers working for Nadezhda von Meck, Tchaikovsky’s patron, playing chamber music and teaching her children. Travel with her household took him to Italy and Russia. In Paris he accompanied the soprano Marie Vasnier, with whom he had an affair, and wrote songs for her flexible high voice. In their accompaniments, the piano’s register, resonance and passing harmonic changes can supply a second interpretation of the words. The early songs also show how thoroughly he knew the French vocal tradition he would alter.
